name: Cornstarch Suspension — Oobleck
use_case: Acoustic levitation, cornstarch monsters, discontinuous-medium cymatics

composition.note: Exact ratio is critical. Too dry: mixture cracks and breaks. Too wet: behaves as normal fluid. 55/45 by mass gives optimal dilatancy.

rheology.behaviour: At low shear rates: behaves as a fluid (pours, flows). At high shear rates: behaves as a solid (resists rapid impact). The transition is near-instantaneous.
rheology.mechanism: Shear thickening in dense suspensions arises from jamming of particle contacts. At high shear rates, particles cannot rearrange fast enough and lock into a jammed network.

acoustic_behaviour.primary_phenomenon: The dilatancy creates extraordinary acoustic phenomena. When driven at audio frequencies on a speaker membrane, the cornstarch develops 'fingers' — stable column-like protrusions that form at acoustic antinodes.
acoustic_behaviour.finger_formation_frequency_hz: 60–120 Hz optimal; 20 Hz minimum to see formation
acoustic_behaviour.finger_morphology: Conical columns that stretch upward from the surface. Unlike ferrofluid spikes (which are stable), cornstarch fingers periodically extend and retract — each finger has a 'lifetime' of 0.5–2 seconds before collapsing and reforming elsewhere.
acoustic_behaviour.pattern_type: Nodal geometry similar to Faraday waves, but in a discontinuous medium — the columns are in the antinode positions (high amplitude), not the nodes. This is the OPPOSITE of dry granular media.
acoustic_behaviour.why_antinodes: Sand migrates to nodes (minimum amplitude). Cornstarch/oobleck accumulates at antinodes because the high-amplitude vibration locally increases the shear rate, causing local solidification — the solid columns are held up by acoustic radiation pressure.
acoustic_behaviour.standing_wave_coupling: At resonant frequencies of the driving surface, columns form geometric arrangements: hexagonal for most frequencies, square at specific depth/frequency ratios.

visual_properties.appearance_driven: A roiling, writhing landscape of extending and collapsing columns; organic, almost biological in appearance

safety.cleanup: Dissolves in water; avoid letting it dry in crevices (very difficult to remove when dried)
safety.electrical_safety: Keep away from speaker terminals and electronic equipment — it conducts slightly when wet
safety.vibration_hazard: High-amplitude driving (>100 Hz, >100 dBSPL) can launch material ballistically. Use a containment lip around the speaker.

preparation.recipe: Add cornstarch to water slowly while stirring. Never add water to dry cornstarch (lumps). Stir until uniform. Let rest 30 minutes. Adjust: add small amounts of cornstarch if too fluid, water if too stiff.
preparation.test: Punch the surface rapidly with one finger. If it hurts (the mixture resists), it's correct. If the finger sinks slowly, add more cornstarch.
preparation.speaker_setup: Pour 1–3 cm depth onto a speaker cone or flat membrane. Frequency response of speaker must include 60–120 Hz range. Use a subwoofer or full-range speaker in a sealed cabinet.
preparation.film: The dynamics change rapidly. Use high-speed video (120–240 fps) to capture finger formation and collapse.

relation_to_cymatics.comparison_with_sand: Sand = dry granular, migrates to NODES. Cornstarch = wet dilatant, accumulates at ANTINODES. The pattern geometry is the same; the phase is inverted — you see the antinodes instead of the nodes.
relation_to_cymatics.comparison_with_water: Water forms Faraday standing waves (periodic, symmetric). Cornstarch forms discontinuous columns (irregular, organic-looking). The column positions trace the antinode map, but individual columns have stochastic lifetimes.
relation_to_cymatics.sacred_interpretation: The cornstarch demonstrates that the pattern is in the field, not in the medium. Whether the medium is sand (which avoids vibration) or cornstarch (which clings to vibration), the underlying acoustic geometry is the same — expressed with inverted polarity.

sources: Merkt, F.S. et al. (2004). Persistent holes in a fluid. Physical Review Letters, 92(18), 184501.
Deegan, R.D. et al. (2004). Wavy and rough cracks in silicon wafers from a wiggling crack tip. Physical Review E, 67, 066209.
Ebata, H. et al. (2012). Dynamical transition in a dense suspension of cornstarch in water. Physical Review Letters, 109, 014502.
